extracted.intended_audience: manufacturers/applicants seeking CMS new technology add-on payments (NTAP); health care providers, payers, and public commenters participating in NTAP rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria used by CMS to assess New Technology Add-on Payment (NTAP) applications, including the newness, cost, and substantial clinical improvement criteria and related evidentiary expectations. Intended to guide applicants and commenters on what information and evidence CMS considers when deciding FY 2027 NTAP approvals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newness Criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the technology is new (commercially available) and when it first became available for sale; CMS considers the market availability date and causes of any delay in commercial availability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must provide the date the technology first became available for sale and explain causes of any delay in commercial availability (e.g., establishing commercial infrastructure, import logistics, U.S. market compliance). If technologies are substantially similar, CMS uses the earliest market availability date among the technologies as the beginning of the newness period (example: if RAPIBLYK is substantially similar to esmolol, newness period would begin on December 31, 1986, the date esmolol received FDA approval). Public comments on newness timing are invited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial Similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of whether the candidate technology is substantially similar to existing technologies based on mechanism of action, MS-DRG assignment, and the type of disease/patient population treated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS compares mechanism of action (noting that differences in metabolism/PK do not necessarily constitute a different mechanism), MS-DRG mapping (same MS-DRG suggests similarity), and whether the technology treats the same or a new patient population/disease. Example: CMS concluded RAPIBLYK and esmolol may be substantially similar because both block β1-adrenergic receptors, map to the same MS-DRG, and treat adult SVT patients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost Criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the technology meets the cost criterion for NTAP (i.e., is sufficiently costly to qualify under program rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS evaluates the cost impact and indicates agreement or disagreement; in the provided examples CMS agreed with applicants for some technologies that they met the cost criterion. Public comments on whether the technology meets the cost criterion are solicited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial Clinical Improvement Criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the technology provides a substantial clinical improvement over existing technologies, either by offering treatment for patients unresponsive to or ineligible for current treatments or by demonstrating improved clinical outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must provide evidence demonstrating improved clinical outcomes (e.g., reduced mortality, reduced clinically significant adverse events per §412.87(b)(1)(ii)(C)(1), reduced ICU/hospital length of stay, improved disease-specific endpoints). CMS requires specific outcomes to be identified and supported by evidence; claims without supporting evidence are insufficient. CMS will solicit public comments on this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary Sufficiency and Quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The type and quality of clinical evidence CMS considers sufficient to support claims of newness or substantial clinical improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials and well-designed comparative studies are stronger evidence. Observational, retrospective, small-sample, open-label, or physician-preference–based studies may be limited by selection bias, confounding, small N, or lack of appropriate comparators. Examples: CMS cited limitations in Dizdarevic (observational), Si et al. (retrospective with physician preference), and small randomized studies that did not measure the asserted outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparator Clarity and Control Definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence must clearly define comparators or control groups to allow assessment of whether the new technology is superior to existing therapies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies with undefined or unclear controls (e.g., 'undefined controls' in a meta-analysis) make it difficult to evaluate whether the new technology improves outcomes relative to existing treatments. While head-to-head trials are not strictly required for NTAP, absence of clear comparators limits CMS's ability to conclude substantial clinical improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism of Action Uniqueness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the technology uses a distinct mechanism of action compared to existing therapies, which can support a finding of non-substantial similarity/newness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences limited to pharmacokinetics (e.g., ultra-short half-life, tissue esterases metabolism) do not necessarily constitute a unique mechanism if the therapeutic target/action (e.g., β1-adrenergic receptor blockade) is the same. CMS rejected the applicant's claim that RAPIBLYK's different metabolism alone created a new mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: MS-DRG Mapping Consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the technology maps to a different Medicare Severity–Diagnosis Related Group (MS-DRG) compared to existing technologies, informing substantial similarity determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a technology maps to a different MS-DRG than existing treatments, that may support non-substantial similarity. CMS noted cases where technologies did or did not map to new MS-DRGs (example: YARTEMLEA maps to MS-DRGs 545-547 and thus was not considered different on that basis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of New or Unmet Patient Populations
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant must identify a patient population that is unresponsive to or ineligible for existing treatments to support a claim of substantial clinical improvement via access expansion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that a drug is better tolerated in certain high-risk groups are insufficient unless evidence shows these patients are truly unresponsive or ineligible for existing therapies. For example, defining 'high-risk' as EF <40% does not automatically make those patients ineligible for beta blockers; CMS expects clear evidence that existing options are contraindicated or ineffective for the claimed subgroup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prescribing Information and Contraindications
rubrics_metrics.description: Prescribing label content (dosing regimens, contraindications) is relevant to evaluating claims but absence of label dosing does not preclude existing drugs' use in a population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS will review labeling for explicit contraindications or dosing instructions but will not assume that lack of a labeled dosing regimen means a drug cannot be used in a population. Example: esmolol's label lacked a dosing regimen for cardiac impairment but that absence did not preclude its use in such patients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical Endpoints and Outcome Measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptable and relevant clinical endpoints for evaluating effectiveness and clinical improvement (examples drawn from submitted studies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endpoints include time to heart rate control, target heart rate achievement, conversion to sinus rhythm, need for cardioversion, blood pressure effects, ICU/hospital length of stay, adverse events/serious adverse events/major adverse cardiovascular events, biomarker changes, and overall survival. CMS looks for statistically significant improvements on these endpoints and clear reporting of which comparators were used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety Evidence and Attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstration of a favorable or at least acceptable safety profile, and clear attribution (or lack thereof) of adverse events to the technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should report rates of AEs/SAEs/MACEs and whether events were attributed to the therapy. CMS uses safety evidence when weighing substantial clinical improvement (example: applicant's statement that AEs were not attributed to RAPIBLYK was considered).

rubrics_metrics.name: Study Design Limitations and Generalizability
rubrics_metrics.description: CMS evaluates study design features (sample size, randomization, blinding, multicenter status, prospective vs retrospective) that affect generalizability and causal inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small sample sizes, single-center studies, open-label designs, retrospective analyses, and use of physician preference for treatment selection limit generalizability and raise concerns about bias and confounding (examples: Koukoulitsios small RCT; Si et al. retrospective with physician preference). CMS expects higher-quality evidence to support substantial clinical improvement claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: When applicants submit systematic reviews or meta-analyses, CMS evaluates the included trials, subgroup analyses, comparators, and heterogeneity to determine support for claimed benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meta-analyses may show heterogeneity or subgroup effects (example: Perrett et al. found no overall superiority for IV beta blockers but subgroup differences by beta-1 selectivity). CMS scrutinizes whether included studies and comparators are appropriate and whether results translate to claimed clinical benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of External Guidelines and International Experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations to clinical practice guidelines or real-world experience outside the U.S. can support claims but do not substitute for direct evidence demonstrating newness or substantial clinical improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS may consider guideline recommendations (e.g., ESC 2024) or foreign experience as supportive context, but requires supporting comparative clinical evidence to conclude substantial clinical improvement or newness (examples where ESC guidance and foreign use were cited but CMS still required trial evidence).
